transcript:
"This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour."
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
The Supreme Court is wrestling with whether a case seeking damages over the costs of climate
change should be allowed to proceed.
NPR's Kerry Johnson reports on the first arguments of the new term at the High Court.
Boulder, Colorado sued Suncoran ExxonMobil to recover money for the costs of responding
to global warming.
That was back in 2018, but the case has still not reached a jury.
County officials argued the companies knew but chose to deceive the public about the
threats from climate change.
The energy giants are asking the Supreme Court to block the lawsuit because they say the
federal government should be in charge of such a sweeping issue.
The justices asked tough questions of both sides.
They seem to be weighing a potential flood of cases in state courts against blocking
cases by Boulder and other local governments at such an early stage.
Kerry Johnson, NPR News.
President Trump is campaigning in Nebraska today alongside Republican Senator Pete Ricketts.
The incumbent Ricketts is facing off against independent candidate Dan Osburn in the race.
Democrats withdrew their candidate to throw their support behind Osburn.
Trump says his visit is part of a 32-day campaign blitz and that he'll stump in Michigan later
this month.
But as NPR's Franco Ordonez reports, Trump says he may not go to all the battleground
states.
President Trump has repeatedly promised that he would campaign to support Republicans in
35 of the most competitive races.
But so far, he's largely stuck to more comfortable red states like Oklahoma and Texas.
As he left the White House for a campaign trip to Nebraska, Trump insisted that he'll
visit more swing states, but maybe not all of them.
He hedged on plans for Maine, but said they'll be going to Michigan this month.
Trump argued that Republicans' numbers go up when he visits a state, but some Republicans
in swing states have sought to distance themselves from the president in an effort to appeal
to more moderate voters.
Franco, Ordonez, NPR News, the White House.
Republican super PACs have canceled millions of dollars of planned spending in North Carolina's
U.S. Senate race.
As NPR's Stephen Fowler reports, some of the money is being redirected to an unexpectedly
competitive race in Kansas.
According to ad tracking firm Ad Impact, more than $16 million in future reservations for
North Carolina's Senate race have been canceled since Friday.
Polls show the Democratic candidate Roy Cooper with a sizable lead there over the Republican,
Michael Wattley.
Some of that money has been redirected to the Senate race in Kansas.
It's one of many Midwestern states where rising fuel costs and Trump administration policies
like tariffs have hit hardest, and where enough voters say they've soured on Republicans to
make these reliably red states competitive.
Stephen Fowler, NPR News.
U.S. stocks rose near their records today.
The S&P 500 added more than half a percent near its all-time high set over the summer.
The Dow rose less than a quarter percent, and the NASDAQ climbed more than one percent
to set a record of its own.
This is NPR.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez announced a snap election will be held at the end of
November.
It comes after his government suffered a bruising legislative defeat last week over emergency
measures to address the country's housing crisis, protesters have demanded government
action on housing affordability amid outrage over the televised eviction of an 87-year-old
woman in Madrid last month.
A company that helps military veterans qualify for disability benefits is being accused of
fraud by attorneys general in New York and Illinois.
Trajector Medical charges vets as much as $20,000 each, but authorities say such help
is supposed to be free under federal law.
The crackdown follows an NPR investigation, NPR's Chris Arnold reports.
The AG say one thing that they're investigating is the company's use of a robo-dialer system
that we uncovered in our reporting.
It calls the VA and poses as the veteran so it can send bills to thousands of vets.
That's even if Trajector didn't actually help them to get disability pay.
We also now know that Trajector made nearly $280 million in income just last year.
Justin Ingram is a former Army Ranger and combat vet who felt taken advantage of.
It's a mind-blowing amount of money.
It's inconceivable that somebody made that much money.
Like, there's a problem somewhere in the system, right?
Trajector told NPR in a statement, quote, "We stand behind how we operate and we're
focused on the veterans we serve."
Chris Arnold, NPR News.
The FDA is recalling more than 122,000 cases of Gatorade because of an undeclared food
dye in the drink in more than two dozen states.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
This message comes from Lisa and their lineup of beautifully crafted mattresses tailored

topics.text: Supreme Court hears arguments on whether Boulder Colorado can sue ExxonMobil over climate change costs
President Trump campaigns in Nebraska with Senator Pete Ricketts, says he may skip some swing states
Republican super PACs cancel $16 million in North Carolina Senate race spending, redirect to Kansas
U.S. stock markets rise near record levels, S&P 500 and NASDAQ set new highs
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez announces snap election for end of November over housing crisis
Trajector Medical accused of fraud by New York and Illinois attorneys general for charging veterans
FDA recalls over 122,000 cases of Gatorade due to undeclared food dye in multiple states
